newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Dobrev made brave bid to defuse crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Dobrev made brave bid to defuse crisis.

text.p: The man at the centre of Bulgaria's political crisis, Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, tried and failed to defuse tensions by suggesting a face-saving way for the Socialists to drop their insistence on forming a cabinet.

After nearly four weeks of daily mass protests against the Socialists' plans to stay in power, Dobrev proposed on Friday that President Petar Stoyanov should be asked to appoint a coalition government.
He told Reuters in an interview the economic and political crisis had now got beyond party politics and he was willing to give up his mandate to form a cabinet for the sake of consensus.
News of his remarks sent shockwaves through the Socialist party, which is made up largely of ex-communists, and Dobrev was forced to postpone a meeting with Stoyanov on Friday afternoon.
Opposition leaders said all it proved was that he could find no one prepared to risk joining his cabinet.
The Socialists are deeply divided between those who want to give up Dobrev's mandate and those who insist on forming a new government regardless of the public opposition.

Dobrev's appeal apparently failed and the Socialists are likely to name a cabinet on Monday, a move certain to escalate tensions that have brought protesting workers, students and opposition supporters onto the streets every day for a month.
"I think the country now needs a constitutional government on a very wide political base," Dobrev said on Friday.

"I don't mind if it is formed under the leadership of the president as I highly respect the president's efforts to find a way out of the crisis. I am ready to return my mandate if such a government is formed."

His break with party orthodoxy stunned his colleagues. The head of the Socialist press office accused Reuters of inventing the interview and party leader Georgi Parvanov said he thought there must have been a problem with the translation.
But Dobrev stood by his remarks and the financial weekly Kapital published the Bulgarian transcript on Sunday as the Socialists met to discuss their next move.
Dobrev, 49, came into the limelight in May 1996 when he became interior minister after his predecessor Lyubomir Nachev was dismissed for failing to deal with escalating crime.

He emerged as an outspoken critic of outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov in December when he attacked the cabinet's record in handling the country's economic and social crisis and raised the previously taboo issue of government corruption.

A mining engineer by training, he was a leader of the Communist youth organisation Komsomol before 1989 and is married with two children. Tall and soft-spoken, with dark-ringed eyes, he usually prefers to avoid public exposure.
Dobrev has been organisational secretary in the Socialist Party and has chaired parliament's national security committee.
He has a reputation as a party strongman due to the access to information provided by his posts. Communist-era police files have never been made public as they were in East Germany.

The opposition holds Dobrev responsible for clashes outside parliament on the night of January 10, when opposition protesters ransacked parliament after the Socialists refused to vote on an opposition proposal for early general elections.
"I am not interested in politics when I am working in this ministry," he told Reuters. "All I'm doing here is to fight crime."
